newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala rebel resettlement stumbles in jungle.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala rebel resettlement stumbles in jungle.

text.p: A group of 70 ex-rebels who hoped to resettle in a jungle farming cooperative faced the still open wounds of Guatemala's 36-year civil war when their neighbours expelled them.

"Who did the killing? The army. Who provoked the army? The guerrillas," Nicholas Rafael, a leader of the 1,300-member Ixcan Grande cooperative in northern Guatemala that voted to throw out the former rebels late on Thursday, told Reuters.
Many cooperative members, who once farmed side by side with the guerrillas, expressed lingering resentment against both sides in Central America's longest conflict.

The tension in this rain forest region bordering Mexico's Chiapas state reaches back to the early 1980s when the war was at its height and the army's counter-insurgency tactics razed whole communities.

The war was officially over on Dec. 29 with a historic peace treaty signed between the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) and the government. About 3,000 former guerrillas have turned in weapons during several months in disarmament camps and are resettling this month.
Resettlement has gone without a hitch in most areas of Guatemala. But in Ixcan the operation has stumbled badly as the war continues to divide neighbours and even families.
"Our main concern now is what we're going to do with these people. They now have no destination," Enrique Godoy, a member of the national commission for resettlement, told Reuters.
The rejected rebels, like their cooperative neighbours, are indigenous peasants who fled the war into hiding in the mountains or refuge in Mexico.
Earlier this decade the Ixcan Grande cooperative was formed by returning refugees and exiles coming out of hiding.

Many guerrillas worked and farmed alongside the cooperative, or as provisional members. But that was not openly advertised until this year when the URNG called on its members to hand over arms and receive resettlement support under terms of the December peace treaty.
After three months in disarmament camps 100 rebels who had answered the URNG call to demobilize attempted a triumphant return to the Ixcan Grande cooperative on Friday.

But they were greeted with threats and violence. In Pueblo Nuevo, one of the cooperative farming villages, the members of the cooperative tied down a government helicopter and burned the house of one of the returning rebels.
The disgruntled farmers also threatened to burn or lynch a municipal justice of the peace along with the former guerrillas and international monitors from the United Nations.

The ex-guerrillas retreated to the disarmament camp and the cooperative met on Thursday to decide their fate. Thirty who had been full members of the cooperative were accepted, but the other 70 were told they had a month to find new homes.

URNG leaders told Reuters that distant political interests -- such as the army and international oil companies exploring in the region -- were seeking to divide the population by manipulating cooperative leaders.

Attorneys for the former rebels met on Friday to determine a legal response. They have already filed a legal complaint against cooperative leaders for violating the rights of the former combatants, lawyer Victor Hugo Villatoro said.
